meta.title: Who really said "The quality of mercy is not strained; it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: it blesseth him that gives and him that takes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Shakespeare. Portia says it in The Merchant of Venice, act 4 scene 1 — and the lines are in the play's first printing, the 1600 quarto.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The quality of mercy is not strained; it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: it blesseth him that gives and him that takes'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Portia's mercy speech, The Merchant of Venice act 4 scene 1. Present in the 1600 quarto as 'The qualitie of mercie is not straind'.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The lines are Portia’s in The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, scene 1, where she is disguised as the lawyer Balthazar and pleading with Shylock. They are present in the play’s first printing, the 1600 quarto, in original spelling — “The qualitie of mercie is not straind” — so the attribution to Shakespeare is confirmed against the earliest surviving text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Act 4, scene 1 — Portia, disguised as the lawyer Balthazar, to Shylock
Between 1596 and 1598; named by Francis Meres in 1598
1600, London — quarto printed by James Roberts for Thomas Heyes

source.excerpt:
SHYLOCK On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.

PORTIA The quality of mercy is not strained.
It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest:
It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
’Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes
The thronèd monarch better than his crown.
trail: The play was written between 1596 and 1598 and was entered in the Stationers’ Register by James Roberts on 22 July 1598; Roberts transferred his rights to the stationer Thomas Heyes on 28 October 1600, and Heyes “published the first quarto before the end of the year” (Wikipedia, The Merchant of Venice ↗).

That 1600 quarto already carries the lines. The Internet Shakespeare Editions old-spelling transcription ↗ gives them under the speech prefix “Por.” as: “The qualitie of mercie is not straind, / it droppeth as the gentle raine from heauen / vpon the place beneath: it is twise blest, / it blesseth him that giues, and him that takes,”.

The Folger edition states that it “is based directly on the 1600 quarto” ↗, and its text of Act 4, scene 1 ↗ prints the modern wording quoted on this page, immediately after Shylock’s “On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.”
Wikiquote’s sourced page ↗ assigns the passage to Portia at Act IV, scene i, line 179; the Academy of American Poets ↗ reproduces it as Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act IV, Scene I.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: Shakespeare was baptised at Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564 and died there on 23 April 1616; his birth is conventionally dated 23 April, though the actual day is unknown. He worked in London as a playwright, poet and actor, and was a part-owner of a playing company. The Merchant of Venice was written between 1596 and 1598 — Francis Meres named it in 1598 — and reached print in a quarto of 1600.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — it is genuinely Shakespeare, and it is in the earliest surviving printing of the play. What travels badly is who is speaking, and the exact letters.

items.why: The sentence is Portia’s courtroom argument, delivered while she is disguised as a young lawyer called Balthazar and trying to talk Shylock out of his bond — not a maxim Shakespeare offers in his own voice. The Folger text of the scene ↗ shows it answering Shylock’s “On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.”

The 1600 quarto has “twise blest” (old-spelling transcription ↗) and the Folger modernises it as “twice blest”; other editions print “bless’d”, as Wikiquote ↗ does. Modern quotation usually smooths it to “twice blessed”.

In the quarto the word is “straind”, and it sits directly after Shylock’s demand to know on what compulsion he must be merciful — the point being that mercy cannot be forced. Reading it as a strainer metaphor reverses the argument Portia is making.

Wikipedia’s article on the speech records that the scholar Harold Fisch identified a parallel with Deuteronomy 32:2 ↗. The rain-from-heaven image has scriptural ancestry; the sentence quoted here is Shakespeare’s own and is not scripture.

misattribution.truthLine: It really is Shakespeare: Portia, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, scene 1, printed in the 1600 quarto ↗ that James Roberts printed for Thomas Heyes.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The speech is an answer to a question. Shylock has just been asked to be merciful and has replied, in the Folger text, “On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.” Portia—a woman in a Venetian courtroom, disguised as a young lawyer called Balthazar—takes the word compulsion and turns it inside out. Mercy that can be compelled is not mercy at all; it falls of its own accord, like rain.

That is what “not strained” carries in the line: not forced, not squeezed out under pressure. The modern ear tends to hear a kitchen strainer and read it as “unfiltered,” which loses the argument Portia is actually making against Shylock’s demand for compulsion.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the biblical echo
detailsBody: Wikipedia’s article on the speech records that the scholar Harold Fisch identified a parallel between its opening lines and Deuteronomy 32:2, and that Portia goes on to call mercy “an attribute to God Himself.” The imagery of doctrine falling as rain has scriptural ancestry; the sentence itself does not. The words are Shakespeare’s, and they are in the 1600 quarto.
context.pull: “On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.” The whole speech is the reply.
